title: Illustration systems for a product, not a poster
metaTitle: Illustration for the product, not a poster
excerpt: Use one line weight, one palette, and one kind of scene to explain a step. A new character style on every empty state makes the product feel unfinished.
alt: A clothing shop interior with folded shirts, hanging jackets, shelves, and pendant lights. The repeated garments fit a piece about one illustration system instead of a new style on every screen.
caption: One system, repeated, is how a set stays recognizable. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What belongs in a small product illustration system?
faqs.answer: One line weight, the product's own palette, and one kind of scene, such as objects without a cast of characters. Each drawing should explain a step you can also write in a sentence. Store the SVGs with the rest of the brand files so the next screen does not invent a new style.

faqs.question: When should a product screen skip illustration?
faqs.answer: Skip it in tables, dense settings, and list rows, where an icon and a label already carry the meaning. Skip a drawing of the interface when you can show the real interface. Use a scene when a single object explains an empty, error, or first-run step faster than a full window.

faqs.question: How do empty states stay consistent?
faqs.answer: Give empty, error, and first-run the same line, palette, and kind of scene. Change the object and the sentence, not the personality. A mascot that appears only on errors becomes the face of failure. If you do not want to maintain that character everywhere, leave characters out.

markdown:
A product illustration system is one line weight, one palette, and one kind of scene, used to explain a step. It is not a poster, and it is not a new character style on every empty state. When the drawings change personality from screen to screen, people feel the product changing hands. The step they needed gets harder to see.

Keep the set small enough that a founder can recognize it, and useful enough that removing an illustration would remove information. Decoration that carries no step can leave.

## One line, one palette, one kind of scene

Pick the line and write the number down. A single stroke weight, used for people, objects, and icons that sit beside the drawings. A second weight, if you truly need it, is for emphasis inside a diagram, not for a mood. Two moods is how the empty state and the onboarding start to look like different companies.

The palette is the product palette. Paper, ink, a line, and one accent. Illustration does not get a private rainbow. If a drawing needs a highlight, it uses the accent. If it needs a quiet fill, it uses the paper and the line. A peach, a mint, and a lavender that appear only inside drawings will show up next in a slide, and then in a button, and the palette you agreed on is gone.

The kind of scene is a decision about what is allowed in frame. Objects and hands, or simple figures with no faces, or diagrams with no characters at all. Choose one. A scene with a detailed face next to a scene made of flat shapes will not feel like a system, no matter how carefully you match the colors. Faces also ask for representation choices you may not be ready to maintain across a dozen drawings. Objects and a short caption are often the more honest tool.

Google's notes on [people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) ask whether someone leaves able to achieve their goal. A product illustration passes that test when it shows the step: where the file goes, which control does the thing, what the empty list is waiting for. A poster passes a different test. It sets a mood for a campaign. Hang the poster on the marketing page if you want. Keep it out of the empty states, or redraw the idea in the product's line and palette so the product stays one place.

## Use the drawing to explain a step

Before you commission a scene, write the sentence the scene is responsible for. "Drop the file here." "This list is empty until you invite a teammate." "The card failed, and billing is where you fix it." If you cannot write the sentence, you do not need the drawing yet.

The drawing and the sentence sit together. The sentence carries the meaning for anyone who does not see the drawing, including people using a screen reader when the image is informative. If the sentence already says everything, the image can be decorative and hidden from assistive technology. If the image adds a step the sentence lacks, either move that step into the sentence or give the image a text alternative that includes it. Do not leave the only copy of the instruction inside a picture.

Show the product, simplified, rather than a metaphor that needs its own explanation. A folder and an arrow beat a hot-air balloon for an import. A metaphor can be charming once. By the fourth screen it is a code the new teammate has to learn. The interface already has objects. Draw those.

Crop for the slot you actually have. An empty state in a narrow column cannot hold a landscape with a horizon, a figure, and a long shadow. Draw for the column. A scene that only works full-bleed will be shrunk until the step disappears, and someone will then ask for a different illustration rather than a better crop.

Motion is optional and rare. A loop that plays in an empty state forever is a poster that will not sit still. If you animate, move one thing, once, to show the action, and honor a request for reduced motion with the still frame. The still frame has to contain the step on its own.

## Empty states share the system

Empty, error, and first-run are the screens where illustration multiplies. They are also the screens where a new style is most tempting, because each one feels like a special moment. Treat them as one family.

Same line, same palette, same kind of scene. The difference is the object and the sentence. Empty is "nothing here yet" plus the action that creates the first item. Error is what went wrong and how to retry. First-run is the single step you want them to take, not a tour of the whole product.

Do not introduce a mascot on the error screen if the empty screen has none. A character that appears only when something fails becomes the face of failure. A character that appears everywhere becomes a second brand you now have to draw in every pose. Either commit, in the one style you chose, or leave characters out. The half-commitment is what makes a product look like a collage of stock scenes.

Write a short matrix: screen, sentence, object, action. Ten rows is a lot. If you have more than ten, you are illustrating moments that a sentence could carry. Cut the drawing before you cut the sentence.

## What you hand to the next person

A system that lives in one designer's head will be replaced by the next stock pack. Leave files the team can open.

SVG for the product, with strokes and fills that use the same tokens as the interface where you can. Outlined strokes are easier to ship without a missing font, and harder to restyle. Pick one approach and note it. A PNG fallback is for places that cannot take SVG. It is not the source.

A one-page note is enough. Line weight. Palette roles. What is allowed in frame. What you do not draw. Two examples of a good empty state and one example of a scene you rejected, with a clause on why. The rejected example prevents the next "fun" drawing from arriving with a new palette and a speech bubble.

Store the source in the same place as the rest of the brand files, in the client portal if that is where the logo and the guidelines already live. A drawing attached to a chat message is how an old style returns. Name the files for the step, not for the mood. `empty-projects.svg` will be found. `blob-friends-final-v7.svg` will be duplicated.

When a screen needs a new scene, extend the matrix first. If the new row needs a new line weight or a new color, the answer is no, unless you are ready to redraw the set. That refusal is the system working.

## Where illustration should stay out

Tables, dense settings, and repeated list rows do not need a scene. The icon and the label are doing the work. An illustration per row is a poster cut into strips.

Error text next to a form field is the same. A drawing above the form, and a red sentence at the field, splits the explanation. Keep the sentence at the field. Let the top of the page stay quiet unless the whole form failed and you need one place to say why.

Marketing pages can be a little more spacious. They still use the same line, palette, and kind of scene if they are introducing the product. A campaign can stretch. A campaign that leaks into the product UI is how the empty state grows a drop shadow and a character you cannot maintain. If you run a campaign, give it a border: these files are for the site hero, these files are for the product, and they share palette and line even when the crop differs.

Do not illustrate a concept you could show with the real interface. A picture of a dashboard, drawn by hand, drifts from the dashboard you actually ship. A screenshot, cropped and framed, stays true. Use illustration when the real UI cannot be shown yet, or when a single object will explain faster than a full window. When the UI exists, prefer the UI.

## A review with the screens in a row

Lay the empty, error, and first-run states in one file, at the size they will be on screen.

- One line weight.
- Colors from the product palette only.
- One kind of scene.
- Each drawing has a sentence that states the step.
- No mascot that appears on only one of them.
- The SVG in the product matches the file in the brand folder.

Read the sentences without the drawings. If the task is still clear, the drawings are in support, which is the right relationship. If the task collapses, the instruction was living in the picture. Move it into the text, then keep the drawing only if it still helps.

Color is the next decision, and it is smaller than people expect. [A color palette a founder can remember](/blog/a-color-palette-a-founder-can-remember) is the next piece: paper, ink, a line, and one accent. If the founder cannot name the colors, the next illustration and the next screen will invent new ones.
